analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 30% minimum tax on income over $1 million.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, the bill has received no committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require households with more than $1 million in adjusted gross income to pay at least 30% of their income in federal taxes, counting Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes toward that total. It phases in for incomes just above $1 million and adjusts the threshold for inflation over time. Almost all deductions would be eliminated for this calculation, with one exception: charitable contributions would still be deductible. Revenue from the tax would reduce the federal deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, indirectly. The tax applies only to households above $1 million in annual income, and its revenue would cut the federal deficit by billions of dollars a year, according to the bill's own statement of purpose. It also removes the situation where some very high earners pay a lower effective rate than middle-income families, because income taxed at favorable capital-gains rates and itemized deductions would no longer drop their total federal rate below 30%.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a 30% floor on the combined federal income tax, payroll tax, and alternative minimum tax liability of any taxpayer with adjusted gross income above $1 million, phasing in between $1 million and $2 million of income so the tax doesn't jump abruptly at the threshold.
It allows only one deduction in calculating the 30% base — charitable contributions — meaning high earners can no longer use other itemized deductions to reduce their effective rate below 30%.
The bill counts payroll taxes toward the 30% minimum, and it explicitly frames itself as a step that would cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year.
The $1 million threshold adjusts with inflation after 2025, and the tax applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income over $1 million a year — roughly the top 0.4% of filers — who currently pay an effective federal rate below 30% because much of their income is taxed at capital-gains rates or sheltered by deductions. Wealth managers and tax preparers would face added planning and compliance work under a new parallel tax calculation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new parallel tax computation on top of the existing income tax, AMT, and payroll tax system, adding complexity and compliance costs for high-income filers and their advisers.

It is a narrow fix rather than broad tax reform: the bill's own 'sense of the House' section describes it as an interim step that can 'serve as a floor' while Congress works on 'more fundamental reform,' and it raises revenue through the deficit rather than funding any specific program for ordinary families.

Critics of minimum taxes on the wealthy generally argue that raising effective rates on capital income can reduce investment incentives; the bill text does not address this, and no committee analysis of the revenue or economic effects was provided.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: a modest deficit reduction and a guarantee that millionaires pay at least a 30% effective federal rate, paid for entirely by the top sliver of earners. The design is defensible — the phase-in avoids a cliff, and the inflation adjustment keeps the threshold from becoming a middle-class tax over time. The honest cost is added complexity from a fourth tax computation, and the bill is a piecemeal step rather than the comprehensive tax reform its own text calls for. It does not raise taxes on anyone below $1 million in income.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 2025, and it has sat there with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act of 2025 on April 1, 2025, joined by Reps. Ro Khanna and Eleanor Holmes Norton.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the full action history shows no further steps — no hearings, no markup, no vote — through the present.

The bill would impose a 30% minimum tax on taxpayers with adjusted gross income above $1 million, phasing in above the threshold, counting payroll taxes toward the minimum, and preserving only the charitable deduction in the tax base.
Both cosponsors listed on the bill page are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households are better off so far: without committee action, no new 30% minimum tax has been enacted, and the existing lower effective rates for large capital-gains earners remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, who face no new tax

for.name: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act of 2025 and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing; the action history shows nothing after the April 2025 referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; with the committee chaired by a Republican, the bill has not advanced, though no vote has ever been taken on it.

industries.note: They would owe a top-up tax bringing their combined federal rate to at least 30%, eliminating the ability to use deductions and capital-gains rates to pay less than that. Their gain from the bill stalling is the public's lost revenue.

Fund managers' income is concentrated in capital gains and carried interest taxed at preferential rates, which the 30% floor would largely override. This group would bear a large share of the new tax.
A new parallel minimum tax computation creates planning and compliance work for advisers serving high-income clients, adding cost without any corresponding public benefit.

The bill strips out most itemized deductions from the minimum-tax base but preserves the charitable deduction, keeping the incentive for high earners to donate. Charities lose that protection under any broader repeal of deductions.

analysis.trajectory: With only three sponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action nine months into the session, the bill follows the pattern of most minimum-tax proposals aimed at high earners: it is likely to die quietly in Ways and Means when the Congress ends, unless tax policy moves to the center of a larger legislative package that gives it a vehicle.
